To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the concentrations of fluorescent biological aerosols measured in the lower troposphere over the US western Great Plains were similar to those observed at forested sites and were about an order of magnitude higher than in the free tropospheric over the same region, and (2) the concentrations were often near typical concentrations of primary cloud ice in the temperature regime where biological ice-nuclear particles may influence mixed phase clouds.

concentrations of fluorescent biological aerosols are usually much less in the upper troposphere than in the boundary layer, but they are sometimes comparable in the middle troposphere, where they could influence mixed-phase and cirrostratus cloud formation.

concentrations of FBAP are often low in the free tropospheric regions of the US western plains, but they are sometimes comparable to those in the boundary layer at temperatures conducive to ice formation in mixed-phase clouds and cirrus.

FBAPs are not as abundant at the cold temperatures that are conducive for mixed-phase and cirrostratus clouds as would be required for FBAPs to be important for ice formation in these clouds, at least in the western US in autumn.
